summary: The article argues that renewable energy, distributed generation, battery storage and smart grid technology are making electrical grids more resilient to power outages, which are increasingly driven by extreme weather and aging infrastructure. It contrasts the vulnerable centralized fossil-fuel grids of the late 20th century with modern distributed systems, citing dated examples and expert quotes. It also covers intermittency, policy and financial support, and consumer participation.
one_line: Renewable energy, distributed generation, storage and smart grids are reducing power outages by making grids more resilient than centralized fossil-fuel systems.
key_facts: Power outages are increasing worldwide due to extreme weather from climate change and over-reliance on aging infrastructure.
Late 20th century grids were mostly powered by coal, nuclear, and gas-fired plants in a centralized model where a failure point could black out entire regions.
On September 7, 2023, a gas plant's technical failures caused a blackout across a substantial portion of the Northeast, leaving thousands without power for several hours.
After the critical outage on October 12, 2023, a significant investment push increased adoption of solar and wind energy.
On December 6, 2023, John Taylor, energy manager of a community microgrid in California, said local solar installations with onsite battery storage kept power on while the main grid was down.
On January 15, 2024, analyst Emily Harris said renewable installations' distributed nature means they can often ride out storms and keep providing power when grid-tied systems fail.
On February 22, 2024, during an unexpected coal plant shutdown, battery storage facilities in Nevada fed power back into the grid and prevented a blackout.

On March 20, 2024, Sarah Griffith, lead engineer at a smart grid technology firm, said smart grid solutions preemptively averted 40 potential outage events in the quarter by redistributing solar and wind energy.
The intermittency of renewables is mitigated by better forecasting technologies and pairing renewables with quick-response sources such as hydroelectric and battery storage.

On April 30, 2024, Dr. Lisa Hamilton, an energy policy expert, said integrating renewables at a scale that affects grid reliability would not be feasible without aligned policy frameworks and financial backing.
Distributed generation produces electricity closer to the point of use, reducing strain on transmission lines and limiting cascading failures.
Growing numbers of homes and businesses installing solar panels and joining energy storage programs form a bottom-up approach to strengthening the grid.
